description: A horizontally scalable, Jellyfin-compatible video server in Go. Every task below comes from PRODUCT.md (features and roadmap), the project plan, compat/coverage-12.4.tsv and the agreed work queue. PRODUCT.md stays the source of truth for status; update this file when a slice merges.

conventions.status: done | in_progress | todo | dropped; passes is true only when done
conventions.priority: 1 is next; done tasks have none
conventions.delivery: each task goes through the build workflow (.claude/workflows/build.js): checks written first and locked, one implementer until they pass, QA and one blind adversarial review with evidence-gated findings, one fix round; then PR, CI, merge, redeploy the dogfood
conventions.differential: a task that adds or changes a route jellyfin-web or another client calls adds its requests to test/differential/requests.yaml, and any difference it keeps to compat/differences.yaml with a reason

userStories.title: Follow any playback end to end, and see why the cluster needed more workers
userStories.description: Serves "Nothing is hidden.". An operator must be able to see exactly where a playback stalled and why the cluster needed more workers, not only that a film is transcoding. Metrics (JS-019) give totals: stalls happened, the queue is deep. This adds one OpenTelemetry trace per playback (PlaySessionId) across the api, stream and worker processes: PlaybackInfo and its decision with reasons; each segment request and where its time went (served from the store, waited on a job, started a job); the job queued, claimed (queue time, which worker) and its ffmpeg runs with their speed; helpers started, and helpers wanted but not started for lack of a free slot; and a failover (lock lost, reap, replacement). The reasons for more workers become metrics too, which autoscaling (JS-057) scales on, so the reason it scaled is visible. Viewers keep seeing in their app that a film is transcoding and why (JS-067).
acceptanceCriteria: One trace per playback session spans the api, stream and worker processes, its context carried in the transcode job row across the Postgres handoff

Given a stalled segment (over 5 s), its trace shows which part took the time: waiting for a free slot, an encode slower than real time, the upload, or reading the store; the stall metric links to the trace (exemplar)
A failover shows the dead worker's span end and the replacement's begin in one trace
Helper decisions are traced and counted: helpers started with the job's speed, and helpers wanted but not started because no slot was free
The demand number and its reasons are JS-164's; a playback's trace shows the same reason for that playback, so why the cluster grew can be read back from either
Log lines carry the trace id (JS-022), so a trace leads to its logs
Exported over OTLP to any backend, off by default; the dogfood runs a backend and the docs show reading a stall from it
Checked with real processes: a test collector receives a playback's trace from three processes, with a stall and a failover in it
userStories.notes: Needs a design review; the homelab has no tracing backend yet (Tempo suggested). Product owner (2026-11-08): wants to trace everything through the pipeline, see where something stalled and why more workers were needed; placed before P6 (Kubernetes). JS-024 review (UX): Sessions can show the viewer's job as done while helpers encode, and no log line says a helper started.

userStories.title: Logging slice
userStories.description: Consistent, structured logs per role with request and job ids, so an operator can follow one playback.
acceptanceCriteria: Each request and job log line carries ids that link them

An ERROR line means a failure an operator may need to act on. Levels and noise are reviewed against the dogfood, and three cases are settled: a library asset store that nothing has yet been written to is swept as empty and logs no ERROR or WARN (D-069; the media scan's rule for a missing root, invariant 56, is unchanged; whether an asset root lost after assets were stored can still be told and reported is recorded and returns as a brief, not built); a Postgres switchover the worker survives logs no ERROR (BL-067); a failed job that a fresh job replaced is not logged as an unrecovered failure, and docs/running.md says how it is counted (BL-167). The e2e and roles tiers then fail on a level=ERROR line in a scenario that causes no fault; a scenario that causes one names the lines it expects by their reason, not their text.
Each line of a playback carries its play session id and trace id (JS-021), and a helper's start, end and failure say they are a helper's and whose
Metrics beyond the transcode path: HTTP requests by role, route and status with latency, store operations and bytes by store, scan durations and errors

Every figure the docs tell an operator to watch is a series on /metrics, and docs/running.md's table lists every series the endpoint serves, compared once by hand with a live /metrics answer when the task closes, the comparison recorded; no test reads the doc (D-069, superseding D-038's 'by a check').

userStories.title: Single sign-on through the household's provider, for Octave on every platform
userStories.description: Serves "Joining and signing in are easy and safe.". One provider declared in configuration. Passkeys and second factors come from it (D-119). Octave on Android TV and phones, and Octave Web, sign in through it by a one-time code bound to the device that started (absorbs JS-180, #296).
acceptanceCriteria: Octave on Android TV (approved from a phone, JS-191) and on an Android phone signs in through the provider and plays; the device holds its own sign-in, with the session, watch state and access of a password sign-in.

The provider's tokens never reach Octave. The return carries only a one-time code that expires in about 60 seconds. The code is redeemed once, by the verifier of the device or tab that started the sign-in, and a second redemption or a wrong verifier is refused.
The journey is over HTTPS only. With real processes, start, return and redemption are each answered by a different api replica. A threat review of the handoff is recorded before Build.

A first sign-in links the local user whose name equals the provider's username claim, a migrated user without a password included, and keeps its watch state. After that the subject is the identity, and email never links.

Provisioning is a configuration switch, off by default. On, an unmatched first sign-in creates a viewer with the policy a new local user gets; off, it is refused with its reason on the page and in the log.
A user disabled or deleted in jellyscale is refused through the provider too. Removal at the provider stops new sign-ins only, and docs/access.md says so.
The journey's routes are bounded per address (D-020). The client secret comes from the environment and is never in configuration or logs.
Every capability it adds is in the published contract (JS-183) and passes its conformance check.
userStories.notes: Needs its own guessing bound, following JS-145's design (product owner, 2026-11-19). D-081: moved from 68 to 36, after JS-178; JS-056 and the tasks at 37 to 46 each moved down one. Criteria, dependency on JS-037 and scope unchanged. Reopens to 30 (after Quick Connect) if a household with an identity provider is waiting or reports it. D-082. Refine returns a brief before Spec on whether an administrator may be linked by name, since whoever picks a name at the provider takes that account. No device-authorization grant (D-083: rejected as a second protocol; a QR, if it comes, is Quick Connect's code in a link, its own task after this one). Refine designs the return so that no token or reusable code appears in a URL, and so that JS-180 is a second form of the same handoff, not a second protocol (D-083, D-099).

userStories.title: Use every GPU and CPU the cluster has
userStories.description: Serves "Growing is adding machines.". What JS-170 (the first slice: Intel VAAPI/QSV) leaves, under D-047's rule: NVIDIA NVENC and AMD VAAPI workers, hardware decoding for processor-encoded streams, and outputs above 1080 lines. fMP4 can't splice across encoder families (spikes/seam: x264 spliced with NVENC lost half the frames), so each stream keeps one family, and its helpers (JS-024) and failover stay in it. D-047.
acceptanceCriteria: Design reviewed before building: how a stream's family is chosen among several hardware families and the processor; what a viewer sees when the last worker of their stream's family is lost mid-film (as JS-170 settled it, or briefed); whether a copy and a re-encode share one slot pool; and whether a GPU family re-encodes above 1080 lines, from JS-148's figures (D-021).

NVIDIA NVENC and AMD VAAPI workers detect by a bounded real test of each stage at start, with nothing configured, and choose per job by D-047's rule (the same picture within its bound, 1.2 times real time measured, within twice x264's bytes, then the least processor; the processor otherwise, logged and counted with its reason). A node with no GPU runs exactly as before.

A new stream gets a hardware family when a worker of it has room and the processor otherwise; the family stays in the spec hash; helpers and failover stay in the family; a seek, a restart and a helper's chunk splice in Octave (or, until JS-190 and JS-150, the native browser check) on each family.
Hardware decoding for processor-encoded streams only where its frames are measured equal to software decoding, per codec and family; otherwise software decoding.
The tone map's curve is the one jellyscale sets in every family; no driver tone map (D-047).

Tested on real hardware in its own tier, chosen explicitly and never skipped: NVENC and AMD VAAPI on a developer machine; Octave (or, until JS-190 and JS-150, the native browser check) plays, seeks and recovers from a killed GPU worker.
Operators see the family and worker of each stream (Sessions, /metrics, JS-021 traces); the overrides are JS-170's three and no more.
An optional GPU worker pool requests nvidia.com/gpu or the vendor's resource through its device plugin; documented in docs/running.md.
userStories.source: PRODUCT.md phase5-library; rewritten 2026-11-08: the product owner wants every GPU and CPU in the cluster used where possible, priority kept in P5; D-047
userStories.notes: The dogfood cluster has an Intel iGPU on each of its three nodes (gpu.intel.com/i915: 1 allocatable) and the user's Jellyfin requests one; the developer machine has an RTX 4070 Ti and an AMD iGPU. GPU tone mapping (libplacebo or vendor filters) gives frames unlike zscale's, so it splices only within its own family. JS-154: the HD 530 cannot decode HEVC Main 10 or tone map in its video processor; software decode, OpenCL tone map and VAAPI encode reached 1.09x in a quiet pod, at 31 times x264's bytes at the bitrate tried. The UHD 630 nodes were measured by JS-163 and are JS-170's.

userStories.title: Kubernetes example manifests
userStories.description: Serves "Installing is boring.". Example manifests an operator applies with kubectl: deployments per role, readiness and liveness, Postgres (CNPG), configuration as plain files. Split from the Helm chart (JS-142) by the direction review, 2026-11-19: an operator cannot install jellyscale today.
acceptanceCriteria: Example manifests in the repository install jellyscale on a fresh cluster with kubectl alone (`kubectl apply -k` or `-f`), no Helm

Readiness and liveness probes per role. Each probe states what it depends on: liveness never depends on Postgres or a store, so a database failover restarts no pod; ffmpeg threads follow the pod's CPU limit, not the node's cores

The manifests size CNPG's max_connections from their own configuration: every process's databaseMaxConns plus the direct connections each worker holds (liveness, lease keeper, and one per running scan, segment sweep or asset sweep pass), with headroom; configuration whose sum exceeds it is refused by a check
The worker's liveness URL can come from the environment or a Secret, and the manifests never put a password in a process's arguments
docs/running.md says which Postgres connection modes are supported (session; a transaction-mode pooler or pgx exec mode, supported or not, by a check), and the manifests connect that way
A replica whose database stays broken leaves service, and the manifests' grace period and readiness lead match the documented ones

The example manifests declare trustedProxies for their ingress (D-020) The procedure in docs/running.md for confirming declared proxies, followed against the example manifests' ingress, says what the operator sees and does when no address is counted (every answer 401, no refusal line), and no sentence there denies a log line the server writes (D-025, BL-221)

Workers are their own Deployment, apart from api and stream, and the manifests' check refuses more than one worker or stream replica on a transcode store or library that not every one of them can reach (a ReadWriteOnce volume), naming the key (D-045) docs/running.md says what every worker must reach (Postgres, each library, the transcode store), and the worker's termination grace matches JS-165's (D-045) The example manifests declare no transcodeCores and give workers CPU requests equal to limits in whole cores (D-064)
userStories.notes: JS-020 (2026-11-08): each worker holds one Postgres connection for its liveness lock, outside the pool, so a stock Postgres (max_connections 100) is exhausted at about 90 workers, long before its CPU (one primary carried 1600 streams on two cores' worth). Connections are the first wall when autoscaling. User (2026-11-08): plain manifests for kubectl are wanted beside the chart, not Helm only. JS-166 (D-067): its docs/running.md part was not written and is carried by criteria 10 and 11 here and JS-177's 'Sizing workers'. From its record, criterion 11's text covers: every role given the same transcodeStore and its S3 credentials; and that a request equal to the limit may not schedule beside a node's other workloads (the dogfood's worker requests 6 under a limit of 12), which is why a 4K-capable worker wants a whole node. D-069: each 'by a check' in criteria 3, 6 and 10 is met by the application refusing or warning at start with the key named, or by the shipped manifests applied to a real cluster in this task's own run; no test reads the manifest files. A criterion that cannot be met that way returns as a brief when the task starts. D-071: the example worker's CPU limit is one the docs' rules hold for (a 2-CPU limit counts 2.0, under the 4K HDR job's 2.08 share). The example configuration names no `transcodeSlots`; whether that key is removed or capped at the CPUs returns as a brief at Refine.

userStories.title: Migrations are safe across a rolling upgrade
userStories.description: Serves "Nothing breaks the viewers' evening.". Split by D-063 (mixed-version playback is JS-208). Every dogfood deploy already runs two versions side by side, but upgrade safety is one line at the end of the plan (JS-058). Migrations run with no lock timeout and no check for migrations a newer version applied (internal/db/db.go), an old worker can compute another spec hash than a new one (ARCHITECTURE.md known departures), and docs/running.md and ARCHITECTURE.md disagree on which role rolls first.
acceptanceCriteria: Migrations take a lock timeout and a version that finds a migration newer than it knows refuses to start with a clear message
One documented rollout order, the same in docs/running.md and ARCHITECTURE.md, and a test or check that each migration in a release is safe for the previous version's code

Observed first with real processes under a playing film: a migration that takes exclusive locks on two tables a running worker and a stream replica use is applied while they run. The upgrading replica starts (it applies the migration again after a deadlock or lock timeout) or refuses once with a message naming the lock; it never fails to start silently. No viewer request is answered an error. The record says what a stream replica answers from memory if Postgres stops just after its snapshot read was aborted; a gap there returns to the product owner as a brief and is not built here (D-063).
userStories.notes: Before JS-054, which adds encoder families to the spec. The version-gated claim moved to JS-082 (2026-11-12). Extended from the Fable 5.2 blind audit, 2026-11-14. When it starts it is split into migrations (criteria 1, 3, 6) and mixed-version play (2, 4, 5) (D-063).

userStories.title: DOMAINS.md defines the domains; each domain's detail lives with it
userStories.description: Serves "Nothing breaks the viewers' evening.". Seen now: every agent reads the 141 KB file on every task and its tools cut lines short. It runs after JS-194, which deletes the Jellyfin-only invariants. DOMAINS.md is 141 KB, with single invariants thousands of words long on one line. Every agent reads it on every task, readers' tools cut its lines short, and it drifts from the code. It becomes the definition of the domains: for each domain its vocabulary, its boundary (what it owns and must not do), and its guarantees as numbered rules of one to three sentences. userStories.description: Serves "The picture is as good as the device and the connection allow."; "Growing is adding machines.". acceptanceCriteria: Spec has a preset, one of superfast, veryfast, faster, fast, medium and slow; it is part of Spec.Hash, so two specs that differ only in it have different hashes, and a spec stored before the field existed reads as veryfast and keeps its hash, so its stored segments are still served

The preset travels in the playlist and segment URLs as the spec's other fields do, so a request answered by any replica rebuilds the same spec and hash whatever that replica would choose; a test asks one stream's playlist and segments of two api replicas and finds one hash

A test with real segments, on local disk and on S3: a store holding a stream's segments at one preset never serves them for a spec of another preset; the second spec's job encodes its own

A measurement test, run as the AV1 rows are, logs for each of superfast, veryfast, faster, fast, medium and slow, from a 1080p and a 4K real-film source, SDR and tone mapped, through a worker's own command, on Ubuntu 24.04's ffmpeg 6.1 and on ffmpeg 9: CPU seconds per second of film, and the time to the first segment and to the fourth on 2 and 4 CPUs; docs/transcoding.md records the figures with the machine and the command

acceptanceCriteria: Observed first with real processes and recorded: what jellyscale_transcode_queue_cores reads while (a) a watched re-encode runs under real time with no helper possible and (b) a play is refused for lack of free cores. If it reads 0 in both, docs/running.md no longer calls it the signal to scale on. Amended by D-048: JS-162 read 0 at one snapshot of each stalling run (case a, once per run); case b is still unobserved.

A gauge on /metrics gives, in cores and for the whole cluster, the demand the workers do not hold, by reason: jobs queued; helpers wanted by a watched job under 1.2 times real time and not started for lack of room; plays refused for lack of free cores within a stated recent window, and, as its own reason, plays refused because the cores are held by a helper another viewer's film needs (JS-161 criterion 11, D-050). Every worker reports the same number, as queue_cores does Whichever replica refuses, a play refused for a held film is logged and counted with the held-film reason, never as cores short or busy (JS-161 minor, D-061).

Each reason is above zero within 15 seconds of its condition starting and back to zero within a stated time of its ending, so an autoscaler both grows and shrinks on it; checked with two real workers for each reason

A second gauge gives, for the whole cluster and in reference cores, the dearest job a new viewer would be admitted for now, by JS-161's rule (one worker or shared). Cores held by a helper of a watched job its own worker does not hold at 1.2 times real time alone are not free; cores held by any other helper are (JS-161 criterion 11). It falls within 15 seconds of a play starting and rises within a stated time of its ending, checked with two real workers, a viewer's job and a helper. An operator or an autoscaler keeps it above the dearest job they want to start without a wait, so no viewer has to be refused or stall to trigger growth. (D-048)
Not counted as demand: a job no viewer watches, a paused job, a copy reading at its own rate, and helpers when transcodeHelpers is off; docs/running.md says which slowness more workers cannot fix
The only label is the reason: never a job, film, account or device

docs/running.md's metric table and docs/transcoding.md describe both gauges with an example alert and an example scaling query; BL-005's missing reason is readable here. Amended by D-048: the example scaling query is on the room gauge, the example alert on the demand gauge; docs/running.md no longer calls `jellyscale_transcode_queue_cores` the signal to scale on, and says why.

userStories.title: A worker finds its Intel GPU by itself and uses it for the re-encodes it does right; the operator sets nothing
userStories.description: Serves "Growing is adding machines."; "Play starts in seconds and keeps up.". The first hardware slice (BL-040): one family, Intel VAAPI/QSV, on GPUs that do the whole job. The worker detects, chooses by D-047's rule and falls back to the processor; operators may turn it off, never need to tune it. PRODUCT.md: any film plays, and plays well; play starts in seconds and keeps up; operators want the server to be something they set up once and then mostly forget. D-047.
acceptanceCriteria: Design reviewed before building: how a family is chosen for a stream; helpers and failover within the family; what a viewer sees when the last worker of their stream's family is lost mid-film (playing on is the goal; anything else is measured and briefed to the product owner before it is built, never a stall or a stop without a reason); how a hardware job is priced against a worker's capacity (JS-161); and whether the task splits (detection and choice; placement and failover).

With nothing configured, a worker tests at start each stage it would use (10-bit HEVC decode, the tone map, subtitle drawing, encode) by a bounded real run, not from the ffmpeg build's list or the device's presence; the bound is in docs/running.md; the result for each stage is logged with its reason and is on /metrics. A node with no GPU, or with none given to the pod, runs exactly as before and logs no error.

A job takes a hardware path only when, on that worker, the path's picture is within JS-169's bound of the processor path's, it measured at or above 1.2 times real time for that kind of job, and its encoder is within twice x264's bytes at equal quality in a quality-targeted mode; otherwise that job is made on the processor there. Checked with a negative case: a worker whose GPU fails a stage (the HD 530 itself in the hardware tier, cannot decode 10-bit HEVC) makes the 4K HDR re-encode on the processor and says why, once, in the log and on /metrics.

The tone map's curve is the one jellyscale sets, in every family; no driver video-processor tone map is used by any path or override. A film's re-encode on a GPU worker and on a processor worker, compared frame for frame on three scenes, is within the bound.

A new stream gets the hardware family when a worker of it has room and the processor otherwise; the family stays in the spec hash; helpers and failover stay in the family. With two UHD 630 workers, in Octave (or, until JS-190 and JS-150, the native browser check): a seek, a helper's chunk and a killed GPU worker each splice, no segment request over 5 seconds, no dialog, the position kept; 10 of 10.

Operators may set per worker, and only these: hardware off (default auto), the device, the most hardware jobs at once. An override the hardware cannot honour is refused at start with its reason. docs/running.md says none is needed.

Operators see the family and the worker serving each stream (Sessions, /metrics, the JS-153 decision line); every fall back to the processor is logged with its reason and counted by reason; no label names a job, film, account or device.

Tested on real hardware in its own tier, chosen explicitly and never skipped: the dogfood cluster's UHD 630s. On the dogfood, each homelab change approved by the owner first (the GPU through the device plugin, no privileged container): a 4K HDR re-encode with and without a burned-in image subtitle plays 10 minutes with a seek at speed 1.0 or above after the first 30 seconds; as many at once on one GPU as JS-169 measured to hold 1.2 times real time each do so; recorded with ids and counts only.

Every capability it adds is in the published contract (JS-183) and passes its conformance check.

userStories.title: My list
userStories.description: Serves "Finding something to watch is easy.".
acceptanceCriteria: A viewer saves a title from anywhere; the list is ordered by when each title was added, and one press removes one.
It is apart from Continue watching, per account and on every device.
Only titles the viewer may see are listed.
Every capability it adds is in the published contract (JS-183) and passes its conformance check.

userStories.title: Filters and badges
userStories.description: Serves "Finding something to watch is easy."; "Their languages come first.". Absorbs JS-046's genres and persons and JS-047's filters.
acceptanceCriteria: Films and Shows filter by unwatched, audio and subtitle language, audio description and SDH, 4K and HDR, genre and person, combined with AND.
Counts respect the access rule.
A viewer's filter is remembered for them.
4K, HDR, audio description and SDH show as badges on a title.
Every capability it adds is in the published contract (JS-183) and passes its conformance check.

userStories.title: Search that finds
userStories.description: Serves "Finding something to watch is easy.". D-148: Postgres first, with no search service until a measurement asks for one.
acceptanceCriteria: Search finds a title from its first letters, and by its original or another title taken from the file beside it.
It finds people and collections as typed results.
When the collection does not have what was asked, it says so and offers titles it does have.
Only titles the viewer may see are found.
A title is still found when its name is misspelled: one wrong letter in a word of 5 to 8 letters and two in a longer word, measured on a synthetic title set.
Every capability it adds is in the published contract (JS-183) and passes its conformance check.

userStories.title: Collections in kinds
userStories.description: Serves "Finding something to watch is easy."; "Their data is theirs.". D-124. Absorbs JS-048.
acceptanceCriteria: A franchise shows as one title in the grid once the collection holds enough of it, with its watch orders across films and shows, and its next title appears in Continue watching.
A list never collapses; a saved rule is a collection that keeps itself up to date.
Collections can nest without cycles, and a title says which collections it is part of.
Collections and their orders come from files beside the films or from configuration.
A collection never counts or reveals a member the viewer may not see.
Every capability it adds is in the published contract (JS-183) and passes its conformance check.

userStories.title: The operator's own ways in
userStories.description: Serves "Finding something to watch is easy."; Goal 5: "Operating it stays boring.".
acceptanceCriteria: Configuration declares named sets of titles (such as Anime or Christmas) shown beside Films and Shows.
A set grants and hides nothing (D-124).
Every capability it adds is in the published contract (JS-183) and passes its conformance check.

userStories.title: Versions made ahead, by the operator's choice
userStories.description: Serves "Storage stays bounded."; "Play starts in seconds and keeps up.". D-120. When and how they are made is the design's choice (D-125).
acceptanceCriteria: Off by default; configuration names the qualities and which titles.
They are kept within a share of the budget the operator sets, are never evicted by on-demand work, and stop being made when the share is full, saying so.
Making them never slows anything a viewer or the operator is waiting for, and yields at once to a viewer's job.
A version made ahead is served exactly as the same version made on request.
Storage is shown per version and title, on local disk and S3.

userStories.title: Ready before Play
userStories.description: Serves "Play starts in seconds and keeps up.".
acceptanceCriteria: The next episode near an episode's end, and a title the viewer is about to resume, start measurably sooner than without preparing, stated and measured.
Preparing never runs unbounded work for a title nobody plays.

userStories.title: Invitations and accounts
userStories.description: Serves "Joining and signing in are easy and safe."; "They see only what they may.". Absorbs JS-033's account rules for the new API.
acceptanceCriteria: An invitation expires, has a use count, and grants exactly what the operator chose (JS-036's rule) and limits, never admin.
Revoking an invitation can remove everyone it brought in.
An administrator creates, disables and removes accounts, keeping JS-033's rules (the last administrator, revocation at once, password rules).
A single sign-on identity is never matched to an account by email alone.
Every capability it adds is in the published contract (JS-183) and passes its conformance check.

userStories.title: What the player saw
userStories.description: Serves "Nothing is hidden."; "Their data is theirs.".
acceptanceCriteria: The operator sees each playback's buffer and the speed the player measured, beside the server's own view of it.
It is kept on the operator's servers only and names no title outside them.

userStories.title: Mixed versions play, and an older Octave keeps working
userStories.description: Serves "Nothing breaks the viewers' evening."; "Their app keeps working.". Split from JS-079 (D-063).
acceptanceCriteria: A worker of the previous version and one of this version serve the same stream, in a real-process test, without a spec hash disagreement breaking playback (or the job is refused by the older one)

With a stream replica of the previous decision version registered and an api replica of the new one, PlaybackInfo offers nothing the old replica would refuse (a real-process test), and docs/running.md no longer requires an order between api and stream

A worker of the previous release is never counted as a partner for a shared play unless it has said it can help: during a rolling upgrade no play is admitted as shared and then left without a helper, in a real-process test (D-061).
An Octave release built against an earlier stable contract keeps working against this server: the conformance check of the previous contract version passes.

userStories.title: One file per task, backlog item and decision, and one order file
userStories.description: Serves Goal 3: "Octave's features have the server they need.", by letting tasks run side by side. Seen now: tasks/prd.json changed in 63 of the last 100 commits and decisions.json in 48, with conflicts between parallel branches reported (monorepo study §1). D-133.
acceptanceCriteria: Each task, open or done, is one file named by its id; each backlog item and each decision is one file. A count taken before and after, recorded once, matches.
One order file lists the open task ids in priority order, and only the product owner changes it. Tasks have no priority field; done is a status, and files never move.
New decisions are named D-<YYYYMMDD>-<slug>; existing ids keep theirs.
One command lists the plan (open tasks in order, one task, the open backlog) from the files; no generated index is committed.
AGENTS.md, the product owner's role and the build workflow read and write the files. Two tasks merged in parallel afterwards touch no shared plan file but the order file.

userStories.title: Octave keeps its catalog in step with the server
userStories.description: Serves "Finding something to watch is easy."; "They see only what they may.". D-148: a change log in Postgres, no broker.
acceptanceCriteria: An app asks for the changes since its last point and gets every title added, changed or removed since then, deletions included.
A point too old for the server to answer gets a reset, and the app takes a fresh copy.
Each change passes the access rule as it is sent: a title hidden from the viewer since is sent as removed, and one newly allowed as added.
It holds after a server restart, a device offline for days, a rename, a delete and a change of the viewer's access, each shown in a test.
Every capability it adds is in the published contract (JS-183) and passes its conformance check.

userStories.title: Spike: films kept as disc images and disc folders
userStories.description: Serves "Any film plays, and plays well.". The owner: disc images and disc folders count as films that must play (D-146). Format support is unresearched, so the spike comes first. No product change.
acceptanceCriteria: For ISO images and Blu-ray and DVD folders, on local disk and S3: whether the server can list the film, play its main title, choose its audio and subtitle tracks and seek, as it is and through a conversion.
What each path costs: reads, time to the first picture, and any storage a copy or remux would take, per film-hour.
Which menus, extras and multi-angle titles are left out, and how a viewer would choose among a disc's titles.
A recommendation reaches the product owner with each option priced, and a follow-up task if it works.

userStories.title: Profiles on a shared TV
userStories.description: Serves "Joining and signing in are easy and safe."; "They see only what they may.". The owner: shared-TV profiles with an optional PIN (D-143). Octave builds the screens (ASK-8).
acceptanceCriteria: A TV holds the profiles of the household that were added to it, each approved by that person or the operator, and switches between them without signing in again.
Each profile has its own history, languages, access and limits; nothing of one profile shows in another.
A profile can ask for a PIN before it opens. The PIN is stored hashed, guessing it is bounded, and it is a parental gate, not a sign-in: docs/access.md says so.
Removing a profile from a TV, or signing the TV out, ends that profile there at once, through any replica.
Every capability it adds is in the published contract (JS-183) and passes its conformance check.

userStories.title: Viewing hours and stream limits
userStories.description: Serves "They see only what they may."; "What can't be done is said plainly.". The owner: parental viewing hours and simultaneous-stream limits (D-144).
acceptanceCriteria: The operator sets, for an account or a profile, the hours it may watch, and for an account how many streams it may play at once.
A play outside the hours, or beyond the limit, is refused with a reason that says which, and when it can play.
When the hours end mid-film, the next request for the film is refused with that reason, and the app is told (JS-197).
A stream that stops frees its place within a stated time, so a viewer who stops on one device can start on another.
Every capability it adds is in the published contract (JS-183) and passes its conformance check.

userStories.title: New-episode notifications
userStories.description: Serves "They hear when something new arrives."; "Their data is theirs.". The owner: alerts may pass through Apple's and Google's notification services (D-145): opt-in, off by default, with no title or detail.
acceptanceCriteria: A new episode of a show a viewer follows is marked for them in the app.
A viewer who turns notifications on gets one through their device's notification service; it is off until they turn it on, and the operator can turn it off for the server.

A notification carries no title, no detail and nothing about what the viewer watches, only that something new is waiting; the app fetches the details from the operator's server. A test reads what is sent.
docs/access.md states exactly what leaves the operator's servers, and when.
Every capability it adds is in the published contract (JS-183) and passes its conformance check.
